topics_covered.title: 1.1 Importance of Physics to Society
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Role of physics in transportation, telecommunication, medicine, energy production, and industrial automation.

• Meaning & Scope of Physics: Physics (from the Greek word "phusis" meaning nature) is the fundamental natural science that investigates matter, energy, space, time, and their reciprocal interactions. Its scope ranges from subatomic quarks (10⁻¹⁸ m) to the cosmic expanse (10²⁶ m).

• Core Branches of Physics (Table 1.1 in Textbook): 1) Mechanics (motion with or without reference to forces); 2) Thermodynamics (heat, temperature, and energy transformations); 3) Optics (light properties, lenses, and lasers); 4) Electromagnetism (electric charges, currents, and magnetic fields); 5) Acoustics (sound production and wave transmission); 6) Nuclear & Quantum Physics (atomic nuclei, radioactivity, and energy quantization).

• Interdisciplinary Fields: Biophysics (applying physics laws to biological mechanisms and nerve impulses); Geophysics (seismic waves and tectonic activity in the Ethiopian Rift Valley); Medical Physics (X-rays, ultrasound, MRI, radiotherapy); Astrophysics (celestial dynamics and cosmology).

• Historical Contributors in the Ethiopian Curriculum: Galileo Galilei (scientific method & kinematics); Sir Isaac Newton (laws of motion and universal gravitation); Michael Faraday (electromagnetic induction); Marie Curie (radioactivity discoveries); Albert Einstein (theory of relativity & photoelectric effect).

• Physics in Ethiopian National Modernization: Hydroelectric generation at the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD, 5,150 MW), satellite communication via ET-SMART, and regional medical imaging infrastructure.
key_points: Physics forms the empirical and theoretical foundation for all engineering disciplines and modern technology.
The classical branches are Mechanics, Thermodynamics, Optics, Acoustics, and Electromagnetism; modern branches include Quantum Mechanics and Relativity.
GERD converts gravitational potential energy (mgh) of the Blue Nile into kinetic energy of rotating turbines, generating electrical induction.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Net external force on a body produces acceleration directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to inertial mass.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Force in Newtons (N = kg·m/s²), mass in kg, acceleration in m/s².

core_formulas_rules.formula_or_law: Kinematics: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as
core_formulas_rules.explanation: Governs straight-line motion under CONSTANT acceleration.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Valid ONLY when acceleration 'a' is constant. Do NOT use when acceleration varies!

core_formulas_rules.formula_or_law: Work-Energy Theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv_f² - ½mv_i²
core_formulas_rules.explanation: The net work done on an object by all forces equals the change in its kinetic energy.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Work in Joules (J = N·m). Scalar quantity; work is positive if force aids motion, negative if opposing.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

book-11-nat-phys_ch_1___detailed.detailed_overview:
### 1. Unit Masterclass: Theoretical Foundations & Governing Laws
Unit 1 (Physics and Human Society) is a foundational pillar of the Ethiopian Grade 11 - Natural Science Physics syllabus. It develops students' analytical rigor, linking fundamental laws and conceptual frameworks to problem-solving strategies and real-world systems.

### 2. Comprehensive Curriculum Breakdown Table
| Section | Topic Title | Core Governing Concept & EUEE Target |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Topic 1** | 1.1 Importance of Physics to Society | Physics studies matter, energy, and their fundamental interactions; classical branches gov |
| **Topic 2** | 1.2 Physics Communities and Their Roles | Master the fundamental definitions of 1.2 Physics Communities and Their Roles, apply stand |

### 3. Integrated Concept Map & Analytical Intuition
```text
[Unit 1: Physics and Human Society] 
       ├──> Theoretical Principles & Governing Laws
       ├──> Empirical Verification & Analytical Formulas
       └──> Ethiopian Context & Examination Mastery
```

### 4. Real-World Applications Across Ethiopia
- **1.1 Importance of Physics to Society**: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Abay River, Ethiopian Space Science and Technology Institute (ESSTI), and Aluto-Langano geothermal expansion demonstrate applied physics transforming Ethiopia.
- **1.2 Physics Communities and Their Roles**: Principles of 1.2 Physics Communities and Their Roles are directly applied across Ethiopian industrial manufacturing, agricultural development, regional infrastructure, and public policy initiatives.

### 5. Examination Strategy & Common Distractor Traps
- **1.1 Importance of Physics to Society**: Frequent in EUEE: identifying branches of physics, distinguishing classical vs modern branches, energy conversion sequences in hydroelectric power stations, and applications of wave physics in medical diagnostics.
- **1.2 Physics Communities and Their Roles**: National entrance examination (EUEE) questions on 1.2 Physics Communities and Their Roles evaluate conceptual clarity, dimensional consistency, and multi-step analytical speed. Watch for subtle unit conversion traps and boundary conditions.

topics_covered.title: 1.1 Importance of Physics to Society
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Role of physics in transportation, telecommunication, medicine, energy production, and industrial automation.

• Meaning & Scope of Physics: Physics (from the Greek word "phusis" meaning nature) is the fundamental natural science that investigates matter, energy, space, time, and their reciprocal interactions. Its scope ranges from subatomic quarks (10⁻¹⁸ m) to the cosmic expanse (10²⁶ m).

• Core Branches of Physics (Table 1.1 in Textbook): 1) Mechanics (motion with or without reference to forces); 2) Thermodynamics (heat, temperature, and energy transformations); 3) Optics (light properties, lenses, and lasers); 4) Electromagnetism (electric charges, currents, and magnetic fields); 5) Acoustics (sound production and wave transmission); 6) Nuclear & Quantum Physics (atomic nuclei, radioactivity, and energy quantization).

• Interdisciplinary Fields: Biophysics (applying physics laws to biological mechanisms and nerve impulses); Geophysics (seismic waves and tectonic activity in the Ethiopian Rift Valley); Medical Physics (X-rays, ultrasound, MRI, radiotherapy); Astrophysics (celestial dynamics and cosmology).

• Historical Contributors in the Ethiopian Curriculum: Galileo Galilei (scientific method & kinematics); Sir Isaac Newton (laws of motion and universal gravitation); Michael Faraday (electromagnetic induction); Marie Curie (radioactivity discoveries); Albert Einstein (theory of relativity & photoelectric effect).

• Physics in Ethiopian National Modernization: Hydroelectric generation at the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD, 5,150 MW), satellite communication via ET-SMART, and regional medical imaging infrastructure.
key_points: Physics forms the empirical and theoretical foundation for all engineering disciplines and modern technology.
The classical branches are Mechanics, Thermodynamics, Optics, Acoustics, and Electromagnetism; modern branches include Quantum Mechanics and Relativity.
GERD converts gravitational potential energy (mgh) of the Blue Nile into kinetic energy of rotating turbines, generating electrical induction.

topics_covered.title: 2.3 Scalar (Dot) Product and Applications
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: A · B = |A||B|cos(theta), work done calculations, orthogonality tests, and vector projections.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.
topics_covered.explanation: Dynamics investigates the forces causing motion. Newton's laws establish force-acceleration relationships, while the Work-Energy Theorem and energy conservation quantify work transfer and mechanical efficiency.
topics_covered.detailed_explanation: Dynamics investigates the forces causing motion. Newton's laws establish force-acceleration relationships, while the Work-Energy Theorem and energy conservation quantify work transfer and mechanical efficiency.
topics_covered.diagram_illustration: Work Angle Cases: Force parallel to motion (θ=0°) ⟹ W = F·d (Max Work). Force perpendicular (θ=90°) ⟹ W = 0 (No Work). Force opposing (θ=180°) ⟹ W = -F·d.

topics_covered.diagram_illustration:
[Diagram: Vector Representation in Polar and Cartesian Systems]
• Polar Coordinates (R, θ): Vector specified by scalar magnitude R = |A⃗| and counterclockwise angle θ from the positive x-axis.
• Cartesian Components (Ax, Ay): Vector resolved into orthogonal components where Ax = |A⃗| cos θ and Ay = |A⃗| sin θ.
• Unit Vector Form: A⃗ = Ax î + Ay ĵ
• Magnitude Formula: |A⃗| = √(Ax² + Ay²)
• Direction Angle: θ = arctan(Ay / Ax)
• Vector Representation: Tail at origin (0,0), head pointing at (Ax, Ay).

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Net external force on a body produces acceleration directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to inertial mass.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Force in Newtons (N = kg·m/s²), mass in kg, acceleration in m/s².

core_formulas_rules.formula_or_law: Kinematics: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as
core_formulas_rules.explanation: Governs straight-line motion under CONSTANT acceleration.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Valid ONLY when acceleration 'a' is constant. Do NOT use when acceleration varies!

core_formulas_rules.formula_or_law: Work-Energy Theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv_f² - ½mv_i²
core_formulas_rules.explanation: The net work done on an object by all forces equals the change in its kinetic energy.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Work in Joules (J = N·m). Scalar quantity; work is positive if force aids motion, negative if opposing.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

book-11-nat-phys_ch_2_topic_2_3_scalar__.detailed_overview: Dynamics investigates the forces causing motion. Newton's laws establish force-acceleration relationships, while the Work-Energy Theorem and energy conservation quantify work transfer and mechanical efficiency.

topics_covered.title: 2.3 Scalar (Dot) Product and Applications
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: A · B = |A||B|cos(theta), work done calculations, orthogonality tests, and vector projections.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

topics_covered.title: 2.3 Scalar (Dot) Product and Applications
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: A · B = |A||B|cos(theta), work done calculations, orthogonality tests, and vector projections.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

• Polar Coordinates (R, θ): Vector specified by scalar magnitude R = |A⃗| and counterclockwise angle θ from the positive x-axis.

topics_covered.title: 2.3 Scalar (Dot) Product and Applications
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: A · B = |A||B|cos(theta), work done calculations, orthogonality tests, and vector projections.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

Dynamics investigates the forces causing motion. Newton's laws establish force-acceleration relationships, while the Work-Energy Theorem and energy conservation quantify work transfer and mechanical efficiency.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
- **Key Principle**: No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
- **Key Principle**: Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.


topics_covered.title: 3.1 Kinematics in One Dimension and Calculus Approach
topics_covered.topic_title: 3.1 Kinematics in One Dimension and Calculus Approach
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Instantaneous velocity and acceleration as derivatives, kinematic integration, and free fall under gravity.
• Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
• Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
• Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
• Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
• Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
• Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.
key_points: Displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, even when total distance traveled is large.
The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

topics_covered.title: 3.1 Kinematics in One Dimension and Calculus Approach
topics_covered.topic_title: 3.1 Kinematics in One Dimension and Calculus Approach
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Instantaneous velocity and acceleration as derivatives, kinematic integration, and free fall under gravity.
• Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
• Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
• Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
• Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
• Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
• Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.
key_points: Displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, even when total distance traveled is large.
The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Governs straight-line motion under CONSTANT acceleration.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Valid ONLY when acceleration 'a' is constant. Do NOT use when acceleration varies!

core_formulas_rules.formula_or_law: Work-Energy Theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv_f² - ½mv_i²
core_formulas_rules.explanation: The net work done on an object by all forces equals the change in its kinetic energy.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Work in Joules (J = N·m). Scalar quantity; work is positive if force aids motion, negative if opposing.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

topics_covered.title: 3.4 Uniform Circular Motion and Centripetal Acceleration
topics_covered.topic_title: 3.4 Uniform Circular Motion and Centripetal Acceleration
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Angular displacement, angular velocity, tangential velocity, centripetal acceleration (ac = v^2/r), and period/frequency.
• Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
• Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
• Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
• Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
• Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
• Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.
key_points: Displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, even when total distance traveled is large.
The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

• Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
• Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
• Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
• Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
• Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.

The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

topics_covered.title: 3.3 Projectile Motion in Two Dimensions
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Independent horizontal and vertical motions, trajectory equation, time of flight, maximum height, and horizontal range.
• Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
• Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
• Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
• Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
• Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
• Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.
key_points: Displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, even when total distance traveled is large.
The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

topics_covered.title: 4.1 Newton Laws of Motion and Free-Body Diagrams
topics_covered.topic_title: 4.1 Newton Laws of Motion and Free-Body Diagrams
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Inertia, F_net = ma in component form, action-reaction pairs, normal force, tension, and inclined planes.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

topics_covered.topic_title: 4.1 Newton Laws of Motion and Free-Body Diagrams
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Inertia, F_net = ma in component form, action-reaction pairs, normal force, tension, and inclined planes.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

topics_covered.title: 4.2 Frictional Forces and Applications
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Static vs. kinetic friction coefficients, angle of repose, rolling resistance, and banking of road curves.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).

topics_covered.title: 4.4 Conservative Forces and Potential Energy
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Gravitational and elastic potential energy, mechanical energy conservation, and non-conservative dissipation.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Net external force on a body produces acceleration directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to inertial mass.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Governs straight-line motion under CONSTANT acceleration.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Valid ONLY when acceleration 'a' is constant. Do NOT use when acceleration varies!

core_formulas_rules.explanation: The net work done on an object by all forces equals the change in its kinetic energy.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Work in Joules (J = N·m). Scalar quantity; work is positive if force aids motion, negative if opposing.

topics_covered.title: 4.1 Newton Laws of Motion and Free-Body Diagrams
topics_covered.topic_title: 4.1 Newton Laws of Motion and Free-Body Diagrams
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Inertia, F_net = ma in component form, action-reaction pairs, normal force, tension, and inclined planes.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

Dynamics investigates the forces causing motion. Newton's laws establish force-acceleration relationships, while the Work-Energy Theorem and energy conservation quantify work transfer and mechanical efficiency.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Inertia, F_net = ma in component form, action-reaction pairs, normal force, tension, and inclined planes.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
- **Key Principle**: No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
- **Key Principle**: Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Work Angle Cases: Force parallel to motion (θ=0°) ⟹ W = F·d (Max Work). Force perpendicular (θ=90°) ⟹ W = 0 (No Work). Force opposing (θ=180°) ⟹ W = -F·d.
```

topics_covered.title: 4.3 Work, Kinetic Energy and Work-Energy Theorem
topics_covered.topic_title: 4.3 Work, Kinetic Energy and Work-Energy Theorem
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Work done by constant and variable forces, kinetic energy (0.5mv^2), and W_net = dKE.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

Step 1: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
Step 2: No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Step 3: Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.
quick_example.result: Newton's 2nd Law ΣF = ma; Work W = F·d cos θ; Mechanical energy KE + PE is conserved in frictionless systems; Power P = W/t.

topics_covered.title: 5.1 Thermal Equilibrium and Temperature Measurement
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Zeroth law of thermodynamics, thermal expansion of solids and liquids, bimetallic strips, and anomalous expansion of water.

• Zeroth & First Laws of Thermodynamics: Zeroth Law defines temperature via thermal equilibrium. First Law (Energy Conservation): ΔU = Q - W, where ΔU is change in internal energy, Q is heat added, and W is work done by gas (W = ∫P dV).

• Four Standard Thermodynamic Processes: 1) Isochoric (constant V, W = 0, ΔU = Q); 2) Isobaric (constant P, W = PΔV); 3) Isothermal (constant T, ΔU = 0, Q = W = nRT ln(V_f/V_i)); 4) Adiabatic (Q = 0, ΔU = -W, PV^γ = constant).

• Second Law of Thermodynamics: Clausius statement: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from cold to hot without external work. Kelvin-Planck statement: No heat engine can convert all absorbed heat completely into work. Entropy S increases in irreversible isolated processes (ΔS ≥ 0).

• Heat Engines & Carnot Efficiency: Thermal efficiency η = W / Q_H = 1 - (Q_C / Q_H). Ideal reversible Carnot engine operating between temperatures T_H and T_C has maximum possible efficiency: η_Carnot = 1 - (T_C / T_H), where temperatures MUST be in Kelvin.
key_points: Work done by an expanding gas is positive (W > 0); work done on the gas by external compression is negative.
Temperatures in thermodynamic efficiency and gas laws MUST ALWAYS be converted to absolute Kelvin (T_K = T_°C + 273.15).
In any cyclic process, the system returns to its initial state, so net change in internal energy over a complete cycle is zero: ΔU_cycle = 0, meaning W_net = Q_net.
topics_covered.explanation: Thermodynamics governs energy transformations. While the First Law enforces conservation of energy quantity, the Second Law establishes the directionality and degradation of energy quality via entropy.
topics_covered.detailed_explanation: Thermodynamics governs energy transformations. While the First Law enforces conservation of energy quantity, the Second Law establishes the directionality and degradation of energy quality via entropy.
topics_covered.diagram_illustration: Carnot Cycle PV Diagram: 1->2 Isothermal Expansion (absorbs Q_H at T_H) ──> 2->3 Adiabatic Expansion ──> 3->4 Isothermal Compression (rejects Q_C at T_C) ──> 4->1 Adiabatic Compression back to start.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

topics_covered.title: 5.2 Heat Capacity and Specific Heat Capacity
topics_covered.topic_title: 5.2 Heat Capacity and Specific Heat Capacity
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Quantity of heat (Q = mc dT), method of mixtures calorimetry, water equivalent, and conservation of thermal energy.

• Zeroth & First Laws of Thermodynamics: Zeroth Law defines temperature via thermal equilibrium. First Law (Energy Conservation): ΔU = Q - W, where ΔU is change in internal energy, Q is heat added, and W is work done by gas (W = ∫P dV).

• Four Standard Thermodynamic Processes: 1) Isochoric (constant V, W = 0, ΔU = Q); 2) Isobaric (constant P, W = PΔV); 3) Isothermal (constant T, ΔU = 0, Q = W = nRT ln(V_f/V_i)); 4) Adiabatic (Q = 0, ΔU = -W, PV^γ = constant).

• Second Law of Thermodynamics: Clausius statement: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from cold to hot without external work. Kelvin-Planck statement: No heat engine can convert all absorbed heat completely into work. Entropy S increases in irreversible isolated processes (ΔS ≥ 0).

• Heat Engines & Carnot Efficiency: Thermal efficiency η = W / Q_H = 1 - (Q_C / Q_H). Ideal reversible Carnot engine operating between temperatures T_H and T_C has maximum possible efficiency: η_Carnot = 1 - (T_C / T_H), where temperatures MUST be in Kelvin.
key_points: Work done by an expanding gas is positive (W > 0); work done on the gas by external compression is negative.
Temperatures in thermodynamic efficiency and gas laws MUST ALWAYS be converted to absolute Kelvin (T_K = T_°C + 273.15).
In any cyclic process, the system returns to its initial state, so net change in internal energy over a complete cycle is zero: ΔU_cycle = 0, meaning W_net = Q_net.

topics_covered.title: 6.1 Coulomb Law and Electric Field Intensity
topics_covered.topic_title: 6.1 Coulomb Law and Electric Field Intensity
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Quantization of charge, Coulomb inverse square law, superposition principle, electric field lines, and flux.
• Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
• Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
• Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
• Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
• Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
• Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.
key_points: Displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, even when total distance traveled is large.
The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).
topics_covered.explanation: 1D Kinematics describes motion along a straight line without referencing the forces causing it. Mathematical equations and motion graph slopes connect position, velocity, acceleration, and time.
topics_covered.detailed_explanation: 1D Kinematics describes motion along a straight line without referencing the forces causing it. Mathematical equations and motion graph slopes connect position, velocity, acceleration, and time.
topics_covered.diagram_illustration: Motion Graph Rules: [s-t Graph Slope = Velocity v] ──> [v-t Graph Slope = Acceleration a] ──> [Area under v-t Graph = Displacement s].
topics_covered.illustration_analogy: Motion Graph Rules: [s-t Graph Slope = Velocity v] ──> [v-t Graph Slope = Acceleration a] ──> [Area under v-t Graph = Displacement s].
topics_covered.ethiopian_context: Highway speed management and braking distance safety standards along the Addis-Adama Expressway are modeled using 1D kinematics equations.
topics_covered.exam_focus: Very high frequency in EUEE: solving free fall problems (v = 0 at top), extracting acceleration and displacement from v-t graphs, and applying v² = u² + 2as.
topics_covered.key_takeaway: Uniform 1D motion is governed by four kinematics equations; slope of v-t graph gives acceleration, and area under v-t graph gives displacement.

topics_covered.title: 6.2 Electric Potential and Potential Energy
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Electric potential difference (V = W/q), equipotential surfaces, uniform field relations (E = -dV/dr), and work in fields.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.
topics_covered.explanation: Dynamics investigates the forces causing motion. Newton's laws establish force-acceleration relationships, while the Work-Energy Theorem and energy conservation quantify work transfer and mechanical efficiency.
topics_covered.detailed_explanation: Dynamics investigates the forces causing motion. Newton's laws establish force-acceleration relationships, while the Work-Energy Theorem and energy conservation quantify work transfer and mechanical efficiency.
topics_covered.diagram_illustration: Work Angle Cases: Force parallel to motion (θ=0°) ⟹ W = F·d (Max Work). Force perpendicular (θ=90°) ⟹ W = 0 (No Work). Force opposing (θ=180°) ⟹ W = -F·d.
topics_covered.illustration_analogy: Work Angle Cases: Force parallel to motion (θ=0°) ⟹ W = F·d (Max Work). Force perpendicular (θ=90°) ⟹ W = 0 (No Work). Force opposing (θ=180°) ⟹ W = -F·d.

topics_covered.exam_focus: Very high frequency in EUEE: calculating net acceleration using ΣF = ma, calculating work done W = F·d cos θ, applying PE = KE conservation in free fall/pendulums, and power calculations.
topics_covered.key_takeaway: Newton's 2nd Law ΣF = ma; Work W = F·d cos θ; Mechanical energy KE + PE is conserved in frictionless systems; Power P = W/t.

topics_covered.title: 6.3 Capacitance and Dielectrics
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Parallel-plate capacitors (C = eA/d), dielectric constant, energy stored in capacitors, and series/parallel combinations.

• Microscopic Model of Conduction: Electric current I = n·q·A·v_d, where n is free electron density, q is electron charge (1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C), A is cross-sectional area, and v_d is drift velocity (~mm/s). Current density J = I/A = σE = E/ρ.

• Resistance & Resistivity: R = ρ·L / A. Resistivity ρ depends on material and temperature: ρ(T) = ρ_0[1 + α(T - T_0)], where α is temperature coefficient of resistance (positive for metals, negative for semiconductors).

• Electromotive Force (EMF) & Terminal Voltage: Terminal voltage V = ε - I·r, where ε is source EMF and r is internal resistance. Maximum power transfer theorem: maximum power delivered to load occurs when R_load = r_internal.

• Kirchhoff's Laws for Complex Networks: 1) Junction Rule (KCL - Charge Conservation): Σ I_in = Σ I_out. 2) Loop Rule (KVL - Energy Conservation): Around any closed loop, Σ ΔV = 0 (sum of EMFs equals sum of potential drops Σ IR).
key_points: Drift velocity of electrons is remarkably slow (~0.1 mm/s), but the electromagnetic field propagates at nearly the speed of light (~3×10⁸ m/s).
When applying Kirchhoff's loop rule, traversing a resistor in the direction of current is a potential drop (-IR); traversing an EMF from negative to positive terminal is a potential gain (+ε).
Ammeters have near-zero resistance and must be in series; voltmeters have infinite resistance and must be in parallel.
topics_covered.explanation: Electric current represents the directed drift of charge carriers under an applied electric field. Kirchhoff's laws provide universal conservation constraints that resolve multi-loop electrical networks regardless of complexity.
topics_covered.detailed_explanation: Electric current represents the directed drift of charge carriers under an applied electric field. Kirchhoff's laws provide universal conservation constraints that resolve multi-loop electrical networks regardless of complexity.
topics_covered.diagram_illustration: Kirchhoff Loop Convention: Traversing with current ──> [-IR Drop]. Traversing against current ──> [+IR Rise]. Traversing - to + terminal of battery ──> [+ε Rise].
topics_covered.illustration_analogy: Kirchhoff Loop Convention: Traversing with current ──> [-IR Drop]. Traversing against current ──> [+IR Rise]. Traversing - to + terminal of battery ──> [+ε Rise].
topics_covered.ethiopian_context: Rural electrification grids by Ethiopian Electric Power (EEP) engineer line resistance calculations to minimize voltage drops across regional distribution feeders.
topics_covered.exam_focus: High-yield EUEE questions: setting up simultaneous loop equations using KVL to find current through a shared middle branch resistor, and calculating terminal voltage under load.
topics_covered.key_takeaway: Current is conserved at junctions (KCL); potential changes sum to zero around any closed circuit loop (KVL).

topics_covered.topic_title: 6.1 Coulomb Law and Electric Field Intensity
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Quantization of charge, Coulomb inverse square law, superposition principle, electric field lines, and flux.
• Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
• Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
• Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
• Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
• Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
• Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.
key_points: Displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, even when total distance traveled is large.
The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

practice_quiz.question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant another identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Neglecting air resistance, which bullet hits the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet hits first.
The fired bullet hits first due to its forward momentum.
Both bullets strike the ground simultaneously.
The outcome depends on the mass of the bullet.
practice_quiz.explanation: Horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity are mutually independent. Both bullets start with zero initial vertical velocity (u_y = 0) and undergo identical downward acceleration g. Therefore, both hit the ground at the exact same moment.

topics_covered.title: 6.2 Electric Potential and Potential Energy
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Electric potential difference (V = W/q), equipotential surfaces, uniform field relations (E = -dV/dr), and work in fields.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

topics_covered.title: 6.2 Electric Potential and Potential Energy
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Electric potential difference (V = W/q), equipotential surfaces, uniform field relations (E = -dV/dr), and work in fields.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.

• Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

• Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

• Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
• Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.
key_points: Action and reaction forces NEVER cancel out because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies.
No work is done when carrying a heavy load horizontally at constant speed because force (upward) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal).
Friction converts mechanical energy into non-recoverable thermal heat, reducing efficiency below 100%.

Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).

worked_examples.title: Worked Example: Projectile Motion Range & Maximum Height
worked_examples.problem: A football is kicked from ground level with initial speed u = 20 m/s at an angle θ = 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate (a) time of flight, (b) maximum height reached, and (c) horizontal range.
worked_examples.step_solution:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity components:
- u_x = u·cos(30°) = 20 · (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s.
- u_y = u·sin(30°) = 20 · (0.5) = 10 m/s.

Step 2: Time to reach maximum height (where v_y = 0):
v_y = u_y - gt => 0 = 10 - 10t => t_up = 1.0 s.
Total time of flight T = 2 · t_up = 2.0 seconds.

Step 3: Maximum height H:
H = u_y² / (2g) = 10² / (2 · 10) = 100 / 20 = 5.0 meters.

Step 4: Horizontal Range R:
R = u_x · T = (10√3 m/s) · (2.0 s) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 meters.
worked_examples.result: Time of flight = 2.0 s; Max height = 5.0 m; Range = 20√3 m (≈ 34.6 m).
worked_examples.examiner_note: EUEE questions frequently use angles 30°, 45°, and 60° so that sin and cos values evaluate cleanly to 0.5, √2/2, and √3/2.

short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Joule heating (P = I^2R = VI), fuse ratings, earthing/grounding, three-pin plugs, and electric shock prevention.

• Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.
